unit.title: Teaching programming and algorithms at university

lesson.title: Notional machines and tracing
lesson.subtitle: What students think the computer does

video.title: Notional machines and tracing: What students think the computer does
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Amina Bello - lecturer in education, Lagos
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: In week six of a programming course, a third of students say that after a equals b, giving b a new value also changes a. They passed every coding quiz. How?
Today: the hidden models students hold of how programs run, the research on novice misconceptions, and tracing activities that fix them.
A notional machine is an idealised computer that explains how a language runs, at the level a learner needs. Students always build some mental model. Our job is to make sure it is a viable one.

Sorva's review catalogues dozens of novice misconceptions. Assignment is seen as a lasting link. Variables are thought to hold several values at once. And students assume the computer understands what they meant.
Here is a short trace. Students with the link model answer seven for both, and that wrong answer tells you exactly which model they hold.

Research by Lister and colleagues suggests a sequence. Students who cannot trace code rarely explain it, and those who cannot explain it rarely write it. So assess tracing and explaining in plain English, not only writing.

Draw names with arrows to their values on the board for every lecture example. Use visualisers such as Python Tutor. And use multiple-choice tracing questions whose wrong options each match one known misconception.
Quick check! b is five, then a equals b, then b becomes seven. What does print a, b show?
Five and seven. Assignment makes a refer to the value b had at that moment. Giving b a new value later rebinds only b.
In the app, open the trace lab. Predict each variable after every line, then step through and compare your prediction with the machine.
Your turn. A student answers seven, seven. Which misconception does that answer reveal?
It reveals the belief that assignment creates a lasting link. Remember: every student holds a notional machine, tracing comes before writing, and wrong answers are diagnostic.

scenes.narration: Try it in your next lecture: start with three tracing questions, each with distractors that match a known misconception. Students vote on their phones. Then redraw memory for the question most students missed.

checkpoints.prompt: b = 5, a = b, b = 7. What does print(a, b) show?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: a refers to the value b had then, and b = 7 rebinds only b.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: a refers to the 5 that b held then; b = 7 rebinds only b.

checkpoints.prompt: A student answers 7 7. Which misconception does that reveal?

options.text: Print shows the last line only

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: the link model of assignment.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: 7 for a means they think a still points at b.
